paras: Have you ever looked up at the Moon and wondered how far away it is? Today we meet Rani, a very curious girl, who finds out how India reached the Moon. We will also learn to use ‘a’ and ‘an’, use the words first, second and third, and become rocket scientists ourselves!
Chandrayaan
There was a girl named Rani who lived in a village. She was very curious and used to ask many questions to her family, teachers and friends.
“Why is the sky blue?”
“Where does the Sun go at night?”
One evening, Rani heard her mother singing, “Chanda Mama door ke...” Hearing this, Rani asked her mother, “Amma, how far is the Moon?” Amma said, “Rani, the Moon is very far in the sky.”
Rani kept on thinking about the Moon and fell asleep.
The next morning Rani woke up hearing the loud voice of her elder brother, Pratik. He was pointing to the TV and shouting in excitement, “Look Rani, India is on the Moon!”

Rani looked at the TV. She could see photos of some machines on the Moon. She heard a few people talking about the landing on the Moon. She was confused and asked Pratik, “How did Chandrayaan reach the Moon?”
Have you seen pictures of Chandrayaan landing on the Moon?
Pratik replied that his friend Vivaan’s mother, Nandini Aunty, is a scientist. “Shall we go and talk to her?” asked Pratik. Rani happily agreed. Both Rani and Pratik decided to visit Vivaan’s house.
Vivaan and his mother welcomed them. Rani could see many models and photographs of rockets in their house.
Nandini Aunty offered sharbat to the children and said, “Rani, what do you want to know?”
Rani replied, “People say India is on the Moon. Can you please tell us more about this?”
Aunty said, “Yes, of course. Do you know which vehicle is used to go to the Moon?”
Pratik immediately said, “I know, Aunty. It is a rocket. I saw it on the TV.”
Rani pointed to the models and photos of rockets in the room.
Nandini Aunty said, “Very good. Yes, a rocket is used to reach the Moon.”
Rani asked, “What does Chandrayaan mean?”
Nandini Aunty replied, “Chandra means Moon and Yaan means vehicle. On 14 July 2023, India launched the Chandrayaan, which landed on the Moon on 23 August 2023.”
Rani jumped with excitement and said, “Can I go to the Moon, too?”
Nandini Aunty smiled, “Maybe, one day.”
New words: curious, excitement, machines, confused, scientist, rockets, Chandrayaan

sections.heading: A. Answer the following.

items.q: 1. Rani was very curious. How do you know?
items.a: She asked many questions to her family, teachers and friends. For example, she asked, “Why is the sky blue?” and “Where does the Sun go at night?”

items.q: 2. What did Pratik say in excitement?
items.a: He said, “Look Rani, India is on the Moon!”

items.q: 3. Who was Nandini Aunty?
items.a: She was a scientist. She was Vivaan’s mother.

items.q: 4. What do the words Chandra and Yaan mean?
items.a: Chandra means Moon and Yaan means vehicle. So Chandrayaan means ‘Moon vehicle’.

items.q: 5. Complete the sentence: Chandrayaan-3 landed on the Moon on _____________________.
items.a: 23 August 2023.

paras: Look at the pictures. One child is on a holiday on the Moon, and another is flying in a rocket. A family is going on a car trip. A grandfather is telling a travel story to his grandchild.
Chandrayaan travelled the long way from the Earth to the Moon. People also travel to places that are far from home.

sections.heading: B. Think and say.

items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary. Sample list: a space suit, an oxygen tank, water bottles, food packets, a torch, a camera, a warm blanket, a book, a family photo, a favourite toy. Ask children why they chose each item. Gently guide them: the Moon has no air to breathe, no water and no wind, so what must they carry with them?

sections.heading: C. Think and say: My travel stories.

items.q: 1. Chandrayaan travelled the distance between the Earth and the Moon. You may ask elders at home about their experiences of travelling to places that are far from home.
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary. Children can ask grandparents or parents where they travelled, how they went (train, bus, boat, aeroplane), how long it took and what they saw. Let a few children share in class. Encourage the words ‘here’ and ‘there’ from the last lesson.

items.q: 2. Have you ever travelled to far-off places yourself? If yes, share your experience with others.
items.a: Teacher note: Accept all answers. Sample: I went to my grandmother’s village by train. It was far from my home. I saw fields and cows there. Children who have not travelled far can talk about the farthest place they have visited.

paras: Let us learn
Read the following lines.
There was a girl named Rani who lived in a village.
A hanky for an elephant.
Notice that we used ‘a’ before girl, village and hanky, and ‘an’ before elephant.
We use ‘a’ before singular nouns that begin with consonant sounds. ‘An’ is used before singular nouns that begin with vowel sounds (a, e, i, o, u).
Look at the pictures. A mouse and an elephant are holding balloons. The other pictures go with the sentences below.

sections.heading: D. Fill in the blanks using ‘a’.
sections.note: Teacher note: Ensure that the focus is on sound and not on the letters. For example, ‘hour’ begins with a vowel sound, so we say ‘an hour’. ‘University’ begins with a ‘yoo’ consonant sound, so we say ‘a university’. Ask children to say each word aloud before choosing.

items.q: 1. ________ dog is barking at the postman.
items.a: A

items.q: 2. My mother gives chapattis to ________ cow every day.
items.a: a

items.q: 3. In summers, ________ sparrow builds its nest on the mango tree near our house.
items.a: a

paras: Now let us practise ‘an’, and then both words together. Look at the pictures: an eagle on a building, a woman with an umbrella, an ice-cream man, and a hen with an egg beside a girl with some fruits.

sections.heading: E. Fill in the blanks using ‘an’.

items.q: 1. I saw ________ eagle yesterday.
items.a: an

items.q: 2. Maya bought ________ umbrella for the monsoon.
items.a: an

items.q: 3. ________ ice-cream man brings his cart in the evenings.
items.a: An (Teacher note: ‘ice’ begins with the vowel sound ‘eye’.)

sections.heading: F. Fill in the blanks using ‘a’ or ‘an’.

items.q: 1. ________ brown hen laid ________ egg.
items.a: A; an

items.q: 2. ________ eagle sat on ________ building.
items.a: An; a

items.q: 3. Mary ate ________ apricot, ________ chikoo and ________ orange.
items.a: an; a; an

paras: Some words begin with two sounds that are blended together. Let us say them aloud: sk as in skirt, sw as in swing, sp as in spoon, and st as in stone.

sections.heading: G. Fill in the blanks by forming words using ‘sk’, ‘sw’, ‘sp’ and ‘st’.

items.q: 1. There are ‘sw’ings in the park. (done for you)
items.a: swings

items.q: 2. The children throw ________ones in the river.
items.a: st (stones)

items.q: 3. I need a ________oon and a bowl for soup.
items.a: sp (spoon)

items.q: 4. Have you heard the ________ory of the boy who cried wolf?
items.a: st (story)

items.q: 5. The blue ________irt matched with the pink shirt.
items.a: sk (skirt)

sections.heading: H. Describing the Moon.
sections.note: Teacher note: Add a large blank drawing box image here, so children can draw the Moon before they write.

items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary. Sample lines: The Moon is round and grey. It shines in the night sky. It has many holes called craters. It does not make its own light. It goes around the Earth.

paras: Fun with Words

Look at the pictures: a sign for the days of the week, children standing in a line, and a child pointing at a calendar. Words like first, second and third tell us the position of something. Who is first in your line today?

sections.heading: I. Read these sentences aloud with your teacher.

items.q:
There are seven days in a week.
Sunday is the first day of the week.
Monday is the second day of the week.
Tuesday is the third day of the week.
Wednesday is the fourth day of the week.
Thursday is the fifth day of the week.
Friday is the sixth day of the week.
Saturday is the seventh day of the week.
items.a: Teacher note: Read aloud line by line and ask children to repeat. Stress the words first to seventh. Children can count the days on their fingers.

sections.heading: J. Look at the words given below. Read them aloud. Find their position in a week using the text given above. One has been done for you.
sections.note: Teacher note: Reinforce the link between position and ordinal numbers by using examples from everyday life, such as standing first or last in a line. Ask: Who is third in the line? Who is last?

items.q: Sunday ________
items.a: first (done for you)

items.q: Monday ________
items.a: second

items.q: Tuesday ________
items.a: third

items.q: Wednesday ________
items.a: fourth

items.q: Thursday ________
items.a: fifth

items.q: Friday ________
items.a: sixth

items.q: Saturday ________
items.a: seventh

paras: Rocket Science: Let us blast off!
Nandini Aunty says, “Rani, a rocket is a champion jumper! But it does not jump with legs. It jumps with a BIG, BIG push.” Put on your pretend space helmet. Today, you are a rocket scientist!
Mission 1: Make a balloon rocket. Mission 2: Jump like an astronaut. Mission 3: Shout in space!

sections.heading: Physics Corner: Mission 1, The balloon rocket
sections.note: Teacher note: Materials: a long string (3 to 4 metres), a drinking straw, a long balloon, tape and two chairs. Thread the string through the straw and tie it tightly between two chairs. Blow up the balloon and pinch the end without tying it. Tape the balloon to the straw, count down and let go! Check for latex allergy first, and keep burst balloon pieces away from small children.

items.q: Count down 3, 2, 1 and let go of the balloon. What happened?
items.a: The balloon zoomed forward along the string. The air rushed out of the back, and the balloon moved the other way, to the front.

items.q: Rocket secret: When a rocket pushes hot gas backwards, the gas pushes the rocket forwards. In your balloon rocket, what is pushed out and what moves forward?
items.a: The air is pushed out backwards, and the balloon moves forward.

items.q: Blow up a small balloon and a big balloon. Which one travels farther? Why do you think so?
items.a: Teacher note: Usually the bigger balloon goes farther, because it has more air and gives a bigger push. Let children try it and measure the distance with a ruler or by counting steps.

items.q: True or false: A rocket needs the ground to push against to go up.
items.a: False. A rocket pushes hot gas out of its tail, and the gas pushes the rocket the other way. This works even in space, where there is nothing to push against.

items.q: Fill in the blanks: A rocket pushes fire and gas ________, and the rocket goes ________.
items.a: down; up

sections.heading: Physics Corner: Mission 2, Jump like an astronaut
sections.note: Teacher note: Take the children to the playground or a wall. Each child jumps as high as possible, and a partner marks the height with chalk. Measure the height in centimetres. Then ask: How high would you go on the Moon?

items.q: Why does a ball that you throw up always come back down?
items.a: The Earth pulls everything towards itself. This pull is called gravity.

items.q: Why does a rocket need a very big push to leave the Earth?
items.a: Gravity pulls the rocket back down, so the rocket needs a very strong push to beat gravity.

items.q: The Moon pulls with less force than the Earth. A child who weighs 30 kg on the Earth would weigh about 5 kg on the Moon. Is the child’s body smaller on the Moon?
items.a: No. The child is the same size. The Moon just pulls less, so the child feels lighter. (Teacher note: Weight on the Moon is about one-sixth of the weight on the Earth.)

items.q: If you can jump 20 cm high on the Earth, about how high could you jump on the Moon? Hint: about 6 times as high.
items.a: 20 x 6 = 120 cm, which is 1 metre 20 centimetres. (Teacher note: This is without a heavy space suit.)

items.q: What fun thing would you do on the Moon because you feel so light?
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary (for example, jump very high, throw a ball very far, lift a heavy box, take giant bouncy steps).

sections.heading: Physics Corner: Mission 3, Shout in space!
sections.note: Teacher note: Ask each child to rest an ear on the desk. Tap the desk softly with a pencil, and then tap it again while the child holds their head up. Ask which sound is louder.

items.q: Which tap sounded louder: through the air or through the desk?
items.a: Teacher note: Usually through the desk. Sound travels very well through solid things like wood.

items.q: Sound needs air, water or something solid to travel through. There is no air in space. If an astronaut shouts, can another astronaut hear? How do astronauts talk to each other?
items.a: No, they cannot hear a shout in space. They talk to each other using radios in their helmets.

items.q: In films, rockets go BOOM in space. Is that real?
items.a: No. In real space, nobody can hear a boom, because there is no air for the sound to travel through. (Teacher note: This is film magic. Children enjoy hearing it!)

paras: Rocket Science: Fizz, fire and craters!

A rocket is like a big fire-breathing dragon! It burns fuel to make hot gas, and the hot gas shoots out of its tail. Let us become kitchen scientists and play with gases, a flame (only your teacher will light it) and Moon holes!
Mission 4: Make a fizzy balloon. Mission 5: Find out what a flame needs. Mission 6: Make your own Moon craters. Then meet two robot friends who landed on the Moon.

sections.heading: Chemistry Corner: Mission 4, The fizzy balloon
sections.note: Teacher note: Materials for each group: a small plastic bottle, vinegar (about 4 tablespoons), baking soda (about 2 tablespoons), a balloon, a funnel or paper cone and a tray. Pour the vinegar into the bottle. Using the funnel, put the baking soda into the balloon. Stretch the balloon neck over the bottle mouth, then lift the balloon so the soda falls into the vinegar. Keep vinegar away from eyes. For a large class, do it as a teacher demonstration.

items.q: What happened when the baking soda fell into the vinegar?
items.a: It fizzed and made lots of bubbles.

items.q: What filled the balloon?
items.a: A gas. (Teacher note: It is carbon dioxide. Children do not need to remember the name.)

items.q: Can you easily turn the gas back into baking soda and vinegar?
items.a: No. When things mix and make something new, like this gas, it is called a chemical change. (Teacher note: Compare with ice melting into water, which is a change that can be reversed.)

items.q: If you let go of the balloon without tying it, it flies around the room. Which mission does this remind you of?
items.a: Mission 1, the balloon rocket. The gas rushing out pushes the balloon the other way.

sections.heading: Chemistry Corner: Mission 5, What does a flame need?
sections.note: Teacher note: Teacher demonstration only. Place a small candle on a plate. An adult lights it. Cover it with a glass jar. Children watch from a safe distance and count the seconds until the flame goes out. Try a big jar and a small jar if you have both. Keep hair, clothes and paper away from the flame.

items.q: What happened to the flame when the jar was put over it?
items.a: It slowly went out.

items.q: A flame needs fuel and oxygen to burn. Oxygen is a gas in the air. Why did the flame go out?
items.a: The jar had only a little air. The flame used up the oxygen, so it went out.

items.q: A rocket burns fuel to make hot gas, but there is no air in space. What must a rocket carry besides fuel?
items.a: Its own oxygen, stored in a tank. (Teacher note: Many rockets carry liquid oxygen.)

items.q: Astronauts also carry oxygen with them on the Moon. Why?
items.a: Because there is no air to breathe on the Moon.

sections.heading: Earth and Space Corner: Mission 6, Make Moon craters
sections.note: Teacher note: Fill a tray with about 2 cm of flour. Sprinkle a thin layer of cocoa powder on top. Drop a marble from about 10 cm, then from about 40 cm, and look at the holes. Try pebbles of different sizes too. Place the tray on newspaper to keep the mess small.

items.q: What shape are the holes that the marbles made?
items.a: Round, like bowls. These holes are called craters.

items.q: Which marble made a bigger crater: the one dropped from low or the one dropped from high?
items.a: Usually the one dropped from high, because it hits faster. Children should say what they actually see.

items.q: The Moon has many craters made by space rocks that hit it long ago. On the Earth we see very few craters. Why? Hint: think of wind, rain and trees.
items.a: The Earth has wind, rain, water and plants that slowly wear away or cover craters. The Moon has no air, wind or rain, so craters stay for a very long time.

items.q: Do footprints on the Moon disappear quickly like footprints on a beach?
items.a: No. There is no wind or rain on the Moon to wash them away, so footprints stay for a very long time.

sections.heading: Space Corner: Vikram and Pragyan
sections.note: Teacher note: On 23 August 2023, India became the fourth country to land on the Moon, and the first to land near its south pole. India now celebrates 23 August as National Space Day.

items.q: Chandrayaan-3 had two robot helpers: a lander named Vikram and a little rover named Pragyan. A lander comes down and sits on the Moon. A rover rolls around on wheels. Why do scientists send a rover?
items.a: To roll around, take pictures and look at the Moon’s soil and rocks, so that we can learn more about the Moon.

items.q: Put these in the correct order: (a) Vikram lands on the Moon. (b) The rocket launches. (c) Pragyan rolls out. (d) Chandrayaan travels through space.
items.a: (b), (d), (a), (c), that is, the rocket launches, Chandrayaan travels through space, Vikram lands, and Pragyan rolls out.

paras: Rocket Science: Numbers on the launch pad!

Rocket scientists use numbers all the time: for distances, days and shapes. Let us count like them! Mission 7: Put the Earth and the Moon on a string. Mission 8: Count the days to the Moon. Mission 9: Build a rocket from shapes.

sections.heading: Maths Corner: Mission 7, The Earth and the Moon on a string
sections.note: Teacher note: Materials: a table-tennis ball (the Earth, about 4 cm wide), a small marble or bead (the Moon, about 1 cm wide), a 120 cm string and a metre ruler. Stick the ball at one end of the string and the marble at the other end, so they are 120 cm apart. In real life, the Moon is about 30 Earths away. Children are often surprised by how much empty space there is between them.

items.q: The string is 120 cm long. How many metres and centimetres is that?
items.a: 1 metre 20 centimetres.

items.q: How many 30 cm rulers fit end to end along the string?
items.a: 120 divided by 30 = 4 rulers.

items.q: Look at your model. Is the Moon near to the Earth or far from the Earth?
items.a: Far. There is a lot of empty space between them.

items.q: Challenge: In real life, the Moon is about 3,84,400 km from the Earth. Read this number in words. How many lakhs are there in it?
items.a: Three lakh eighty-four thousand four hundred. It has 3 lakhs and some more.

sections.heading: Maths Corner: Mission 8, How many days to the Moon?
sections.note: Teacher note: Show a calendar for July and August 2023 if you can, and let children count the days with their fingers.

items.q: Chandrayaan was launched on 14 July 2023. July has 31 days. How many days are left in July after the 14th?
It landed on 23 August 2023, so we add 23 days of August. How many days did Chandrayaan take in all?
There are 7 days in a week. How many weeks and extra days are there in 40 days?
items.a: 5 weeks and 5 days. (7 x 5 = 35, and 40 - 35 = 5.)

items.q: Brain teaser: Chandrayaan was launched on a Friday. On which day of the week did it land? Count 5 days after Friday.
items.a: Wednesday. (Saturday, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday.) Teacher note: This uses the days of the week from Fun with Words.

items.q: Countdown! Count backwards from 10 to 1. Then count backwards in twos from 20.

sections.heading: Maths Corner: Mission 9, Shapes of a rocket
sections.note: Teacher note: If children have not learnt the names yet, show a real tin and a paper cone, and let them feel the shapes.

items.q: A rocket’s body looks like a long tube. What 3D shape is this? Its pointed top has the shape of what?
items.a: A cylinder. The pointed top is a cone.

items.q: Look around you. Name one thing shaped like a cylinder and one thing shaped like a cone.
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary (for example, a tin, a pipe or a glass for a cylinder; a party hat, an ice-cream cone or a funnel for a cone).

items.q: A model rocket uses 1 cone, 1 cylinder and 3 triangles for its fins. How many shapes are used in all?
items.a: 1 + 1 + 3 = 5 shapes.

paras: Look at the pictures. Children are cutting out newspaper clippings, showing a chart they made, and reading a story about the Moon.

sections.heading: K. Group work: Our Chandrayaan-3 chart.

items.q: Divide yourselves into small groups. Each group shall collect newspaper or magazine clippings related to the Chandrayaan-3 mission. Paste them on a chart paper and display it in your class.
items.a: Teacher note: Make groups of four or five. Children can look for pictures of the rocket, the Vikram lander, the Pragyan rover and the Indian flag on the Moon, and for news headlines. Ask each group to write one sentence under each picture. Display the charts, and let groups walk around and say what they like about each chart. Supervise children when they use scissors.

sections.heading: L. Let us explore.

items.q: Do you know a song or a story about the Moon in your mother tongue? If not, ask your family members and share it in the class.
items.a: Teacher note: Encourage students to share stories with others. Accept all languages. Introduce the English counterparts of the words as and when possible (for example, chaand is Moon, taare are stars, raat is night).

paras: Self Assessment
Now it is your turn to think about how you did. Be honest, and tick the boxes that are true for you!

sections.note: Teacher note: The assessment sheet can be filled by the student under the guidance of parents and teachers.

1. I can recite the poems
[ ] in a group.
[ ] in pairs.
[ ] by repeating after my teacher.
[ ] by myself.
items.a: Teacher note: Children tick the boxes that are true for them. There is no poem in this lesson, so children can think about the poems from earlier lessons.

items.q:
2. I can read the stories
[ ] by myself.
[ ] with my classmates.
[ ] with the help of my teacher.
items.a: Teacher note: Children tick the boxes that are true for them.

items.q:
3. I can write
[ ] by copying from the book or the board.
[ ] as my teacher speaks.
[ ] with the help of my classmates.
[ ] by myself.
items.a: Teacher note: Children tick the boxes that are true for them.

items.q:
4. I can tell the stories that I have read or listened
[ ] by myself (without any help).
[ ] with the help of the teacher.
[ ] by using the book.
items.a: Teacher note: Ask a few children to retell the story of Rani and Chandrayaan in their own words.

items.q:
5. I was able to do
[ ] all the exercise questions.
[ ] most of the exercise questions.
[ ] a few exercise questions.
items.a: Teacher note: Children tick the box that is true for them. Praise honest answers.
